items.title: Pods
items.context: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers that share a network namespace (one IP, talk over localhost) and can share volumes. Pods are ephemeral; controllers like Deployments recreate them.

questions.prompt: Two containers in the same Pod reach each other via:
questions.explanation: They share one network namespace — the sidecar pattern relies on this.

items.title: Deployments
items.context: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which keep N Pod replicas running. Changing the Pod template triggers a rolling update; kubectl rollout status watches it and kubectl rollout undo returns to the previous revision.

questions.prompt: A new release is failing. The quickest way back to the previous version is:
choices: Edit the Pods one by one
questions.explanation: The Deployment keeps old ReplicaSets around for exactly this.

items.title: Services
items.context: A Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name to a set of Pods selected by labels. ClusterIP is internal-only (the default), NodePort opens a port on every node, LoadBalancer asks the cloud for an external load balancer.

questions.prompt: A Service exists but has no endpoints and requests fail. Check first:
choices: That its selector matches the Pods' labels
questions.explanation: kubectl get endpoints <svc> is empty when the selector matches no ready Pods.

items.title: Ingress
items.context: An Ingress defines HTTP routing (hosts, paths, TLS) to Services. It only takes effect if an ingress controller (NGINX Ingress, Traefik, a cloud controller) is installed. The newer Gateway API generalises it.

questions.prompt: You applied an Ingress but nothing routes traffic. A common cause is:
choices: No ingress controller is running in the cluster
questions.explanation: The Ingress object is just configuration; the controller implements it.

items.title: ConfigMaps & Secrets
items.context: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive config; Secrets hold sensitive values. Secret data is only base64-encoded — not encrypted — unless you enable encryption at rest in etcd, and anyone allowed to read Secrets in the namespace can decode them. Many teams use external secret stores.

questions.prompt: By default, values in a Kubernetes Secret are:
questions.explanation: Restrict access with RBAC and enable encryption at rest.

items.title: Probes
items.context: A failing liveness probe restarts the container. A failing readiness probe removes the Pod from Service endpoints without restarting it. A startup probe holds the other probes off until a slow-starting app is up.

questions.prompt: The app is alive but waiting for its database. Which probe should fail?
choices: Readiness — stop sending it traffic, don't restart it
questions.explanation: Restarting wouldn't fix a missing dependency and can cause restart storms.

questions.prompt: A Java app needs 90 s to start and keeps getting killed by its liveness probe. Best fix:
choices: Add a startup probe so liveness waits until startup completes
questions.explanation: Startup probes exist exactly for slow starters.

items.title: Requests & limits
items.context: The scheduler places Pods using requests. Limits cap usage: going over the memory limit gets the container OOMKilled; going over the CPU limit only throttles it. Requests and limits together determine the Pod's QoS class.

questions.prompt: A container exceeds its memory limit. What happens?
choices: It's killed (OOMKilled) and restarted according to the restart policy
Nothing until the node runs out
questions.explanation: CPU is compressible (throttled); memory isn't.

items.title: CrashLoopBackOff
items.context: CrashLoopBackOff means the container keeps exiting and Kubernetes waits longer and longer before restarting it. kubectl logs <pod> --previous shows the crashed instance's output; kubectl describe pod shows events and the exit code (137 often means OOMKilled).

questions.prompt: A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. First command to understand why:
questions.explanation: The current container may not have logged anything yet; --previous shows the last crash.

items.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
items.context: The HPA scales a Deployment's replica count based on metrics such as CPU utilisation relative to the Pods' requests. It needs metrics-server (or a custom metrics adapter) and Pods with resource requests set.

questions.prompt: The HPA shows <unknown> for CPU. A common cause is:
choices: The Pods have no CPU requests (or metrics-server isn't installed)
questions.explanation: Utilisation is a percentage of the request; with no request there's nothing to compare against.

items.title: StatefulSets
items.context: StatefulSets give Pods stable names (db-0, db-1), stable network identities via a headless Service, and one PersistentVolumeClaim per Pod that survives rescheduling. Pods start and stop in order. They're used for databases and clustered systems like Kafka.

questions.prompt: Why run a database cluster as a StatefulSet rather than a Deployment?
choices: Each replica needs a stable identity and its own persistent volume
questions.explanation: Deployment Pods are interchangeable; database replicas aren't.

items.title: RBAC
items.context: A Role grants permissions on resources within one namespace; a ClusterRole is cluster-wide (or reusable across namespaces). RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings attach them to users, groups or ServiceAccounts. Grant the least privilege needed.

questions.prompt: A CI ServiceAccount should only update Deployments in the 'staging' namespace. Use:
choices: A Role in staging plus a RoleBinding
questions.explanation: Namespace-scoped permissions keep the blast radius small.

items.title: Control plane
items.context: The API server is the front door (kubectl talks to it); etcd stores all cluster state; the scheduler assigns Pods to nodes; controller-manager runs reconcile loops. On every node, the kubelet runs Pods via the container runtime and kube-proxy (or a CNI) handles Service networking.

questions.prompt: Where is the cluster's desired and current state stored?
questions.explanation: Back up etcd; losing it means losing the cluster's state.

items.title: Declarative apply
items.context: kubectl apply -f manifests/ declares the desired state; Kubernetes controllers continuously reconcile reality towards it. Keeping manifests in Git and applying them automatically (Argo CD, Flux) is GitOps.

questions.prompt: In GitOps, the source of truth for what runs in the cluster is:
choices: Whatever someone last ran with kubectl edit
questions.explanation: Manual drift gets reverted by the GitOps controller.

items.title: DaemonSets
items.context: A DaemonSet runs one copy of a Pod on every node (or on selected nodes), adding it automatically to new nodes. It's used for node-level agents: log shippers, monitoring exporters, CNI plugins.

questions.prompt: A log collector must run on every node. Use a:
questions.explanation: Replica counts don't follow nodes; DaemonSets do.

items.title: Jobs & CronJobs
items.context: A Job runs Pods until a task completes successfully (with retries via backoffLimit). A CronJob creates Jobs on a cron schedule — for backups, reports and cleanups.

questions.prompt: A nightly database backup in Kubernetes should be a:
questions.explanation: Deployments are for long-running processes that should always be up.

items.title: Persistent storage
items.context: A PersistentVolumeClaim requests storage; a StorageClass provisions a matching PersistentVolume dynamically (an EBS volume, a disk). The Pod mounts the claim, and the data outlives the Pod. Access modes such as ReadWriteOnce limit how many nodes can mount it.

questions.prompt: How does a Pod usually get a cloud disk in Kubernetes?
choices: It references a PVC, which a StorageClass fulfils dynamically
It downloads the disk at start-up
questions.explanation: The PVC decouples the app from the storage details.

items.title: Taints & tolerations
items.context: A taint on a node repels Pods that don't tolerate it (e.g. GPU nodes, or control-plane nodes tainted NoSchedule). Tolerations let specific Pods be scheduled there; node affinity or nodeSelector then attracts them to those nodes.

questions.prompt: GPU nodes should only run GPU workloads. Configure:
choices: A taint on the GPU nodes plus a toleration (and node affinity) on GPU Pods
A bigger CPU request on every Pod
questions.explanation: Taints keep others off; affinity pulls the right Pods on.

items.title: Rolling update settings
items.context: A Deployment's rolling update uses maxSurge (extra Pods allowed above the desired count) and maxUnavailable (how many may be down during the update). maxUnavailable: 0 with maxSurge: 1 keeps full capacity, adding one new Pod at a time.

questions.prompt: To never drop below full capacity during a rollout, set:
questions.explanation: Readiness probes decide when each new Pod counts as available.

items.title: Helm
items.context: Helm packages Kubernetes manifests as charts with templates and values.yaml. helm install / upgrade creates a release with numbered revisions; helm rollback returns to an earlier revision. Override settings per environment with -f values-prod.yaml.

questions.prompt: With Helm, how do you vary replica counts between staging and production?
choices: Fork the chart for each environment
questions.explanation: One chart, several value sets.

items.title: Port-forwarding
items.context: kubectl port-forward svc/api 8080:80 tunnels a local port to a Service or Pod through the API server — handy for debugging without exposing anything publicly.

questions.prompt: To hit an internal ClusterIP service from your laptop temporarily:
questions.explanation: It only lasts while the command runs.

items.title: ImagePullBackOff
items.context: ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull means the kubelet couldn't pull the image: a wrong name or tag, a private registry without imagePullSecrets, missing permissions, or a rate limit. kubectl describe pod shows the exact error.

questions.prompt: A new Pod is stuck in ImagePullBackOff. Most likely:
choices: Wrong image name/tag or missing registry credentials
questions.explanation: The container never starts, so app logs are empty.
